description_full: Lennox International Inc., together with its subsidiaries, designs, manufactures, and markets products for the heating, ventilation, air conditioning, and refrigeration markets in the United States, Canada, and internationally. The Home Comfort Solutions segment provides furnaces, air conditioners, heat pumps, packaged heating and cooling systems, indoor air quality equipment, comfort control products, and replacement parts and supplies; residential heating, ventilation, cooling equipment, and air conditioning; and evaporator coils, air handlers, and unit heaters under the Lennox, Dave Lennox Signature Collection, Armstrong Air, Ducane, AirEase, Concord, MagicPak, Advanced Distributor Products, Allied, Elite Series, Supco, Linebacker, Elite series, Merit Series, Comfort Sync, Healthy Climate, Healthy Climate Solutions, iComfort, ComfortSense, and Lennox Stores names. The Building Climate Solutions segment offers unitary heating and air conditioning equipment, controls, installation and service of commercial heating and cooling equipment, variable refrigerant flow commercial, curb, curb adapters, drop box diffusers, HVAC recycling, and salvage service. This segment also provides condensing units, unit coolers, fluid coolers, air cooled condensers, process chillers, compressorized racks, and replacement parts and supplies under the Lennox, Model L, CORE, Enlight, Xion, Energence, Prodigy, Strategos, Raider, Lennox VRF, Lennox National Account Services, Allied Commercial, Duro Dyne, Dyne-Tite, Durozone, Elite, AES Industries, Mechanical, Heatcraft Worldwide Refrigeration, Bohn, MAGNA, Larkin, Climate Control, Chandler Refrigeration, IntelliGen, and Interlink brands. The company also offers small package units, rooftop units, chillers, air handlers, and fan coils. It sells its products and services through direct sales, distributors, and company-owned parts and supplies stores. The company was founded in 1895 and is headquartered in Richardson, Texas.

financial_summary: Lennox International, Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $12.0B market cap on $5.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 48% against a 9% cost of capital — a 39-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 28%.

The business throws off $639M in free cash flow — roughly 12 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.94× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 25× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 5.4% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 9.7% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.

Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 11pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.80x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 26% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 40% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 1.08, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $175.7M traded a day, and interest is running hot at 1.5x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 36% in the 2020 crash, 41% in the 2022 bear market and 51% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $335 (margin of safety -5%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 6%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $246 to $463 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 15.9 vs 24.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 22% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $372 on average, 6% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 48% clears the cost of capital of 9.4% by 39pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.41).
It runs a 28% gross margin and converts 12% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 69% is amplified by 3.5x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 2.0% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA ($34.7M of cash against $1.4B of debt), with interest covered 25.5x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.5, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.3% over 3 years, 7.4% over 5 years and 4.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 18% of profits supports about 8.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 3.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 2.3% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 19, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 9.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 82%.
It returns 5.4% a year to shareholders (4.0% in buybacks and 1.5% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 26 consecutive years, raising it 7.9% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 10.1% of the float, 4.0 days to cover.
people: With about 5,400 employees, each generates about $962K of revenue, 2.7x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 3.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $118K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.8M (3x revenue per employee).
